IonQ unveiled the industry's first real-time quantum error decoder, yet IONQ stock remains down 43% over the past year despite a 4% gain on the news.

IonQ (NYSE:IONQ) said Wednesday it had demonstrated the industry's first end-to-end real-time quantum error decoder, letting a single processor find, fix, and decode errors while the machine keeps running. CNBC reported shares jumping as much as 13% intraday on the news.
The measured close was more modest. IONQ finished the session at $42.54, a gain of 4.42% on the day and 15.47% over the week.
Zoom out and the picture inverts. The stock is down 43.39% over the past year and still 5.19% lower year to date. A genuine engineering first has not restored a full year of losses.
IonQ appears to have solved something the entire industry has been chasing, yet the market is treating the news as a relief rally inside a downtrend rather than a repricing event.

Qubits decohere. Errors accumulate faster than a paused correction routine can clean them up, which is why quantum machines have looked more like demonstrations than computers.
Continuous, background decoding is the difference between a laboratory result and a working device. On CNBC's Fast Money, trader Steve Grasso said, "The big takeaway is that's been the problem for the entire industry. It's the real-time error correction because you can't slow down the machine and you have to use the quantum speed but be able to not get that" error.

The bottleneck may be solved, but the commercial model is not. IonQ reported $80.05 million in Q2 revenue and reiterated a $280 million to $290 million full-year range.
That sits against a market capitalization near $17.23 billion and a price-to-sales multiple of 66.97. Adjusted EBITDA in the quarter was negative $120.3 million, with full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA loss guidance of -$310 million to -$330 million.

Between a decoding demo and a repeatable enterprise contract sits a 256-qubit commissioning campaign, integration of the $1.8 billion Skywater acquisition, and a manufacturing ramp dated to the first half of next year.
The Q2 8-K filing shows why the loss line still swamps the top line: a roughly $1.6 billion non-cash impact from the mark-to-market valuation of warrants produced a GAAP net loss of about $1.9 billion.
Grasso conceded the point while recommending the sector: "They burn a ton of cash. The whole industry" does.
For a company with no revenue engine to fund its roadmap, the single recurring event that matters more than any technical first is the next capital raise. IonQ closed a $2 billion equity offering last October, lifting pro forma cash to near $3.5 billion.
A breakthrough is frequently the best moment to issue equity, because the tape supports the price and demand is deep. Existing holders should expect another capital raise.
Share count is already near 405.1 million, and stock-based compensation ran $141.8 million in the quarter alone.
Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) fell 3.12% in the session, and D-Wave Quantum (NASDAQ:QBTS) dropped 4.27%, while IonQ rose, which runs counter to a basket trade.
Either the market decided quantum is winner-take-most, or funds financed the IonQ leg by selling the neighbors. Both readings undercut Grasso's suggestion to own a basket of these names.
Courtney Garcia's counterpoint deserves the last word on positioning: quantum works alongside AI, and the picks-and-shovels beneficiary is the company already earning from the ecosystem.
NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) closed at $225.51 and is up 26.69% over the past year, which is how the market prices proven cash generation against promised cash generation.

Analyst sentiment supports the thesis: 10 Buy, 1 Strong Buy, 2 Hold, and no Sell ratings, with an average target of $67.14 as of this writing.

pages.text:
The cash IonQ burned in half a year was only half a day's worth of Microsoft's core business earnings — Reading an article titled 'Microsoft is better for quantum' through the lens of budget allocation
On September 29, the U.S. investment research firm Zacks published an article comparing IonQ and Microsoft (also reprinted on Yahoo Finance). The title was 'Which Quantum Stock Has More Upside in October?' The conclusion was clear: if you are investing in quantum for October, Microsoft is in a better position.
There are two reasons. Microsoft earns significant profits from its core business, and it can use that cash to continue quantum research for a long time. Its stock price relative to sales is also much more stable than IonQ's. While IonQ is growing in both technology and sales, it is operating at a loss and cannot cover the time it takes for quantum to become a viable business with the money it earns itself.
As someone who has the majority of their assets in IonQ, I wanted to skip the article as soon as I saw the title. I could already see the conclusion that my holdings were at a disadvantage. What caught my attention when I opened it was that the distinction between 'a company that can bet on quantum with cash from its core business' and 'a company that cannot generate its own funds until quantum becomes a business' was close to the topic of budget allocation, which I always worry about in my design work. So, I went back and checked the figures from the financial reports mentioned in the article.
When normalized to a full year, Microsoft is much larger
The article lists three months of cash generated by Microsoft's core business (operating cash flow) alongside one year of capital expenditure in the same paragraph. Because the periods are different, it reads as if the amount spent is double the amount earned.
When normalized to a full year, even after subtracting all capital expenditures from the cash coming in from the core business, about $67 billion remains. The cash on hand mentioned in the article also more than triples when short-term investments are added.
According to the article, the majority of capital expenditure is for cloud and AI data centers. Research and development expenses also account for about 10% of sales.
There is no mention anywhere of how much is being spent on quantum. As far as I read in the business description and R&D sections of the annual report (10-K), I could not even find the word 'quantum.' Microsoft's quantum expenses are buried somewhere within R&D or capital expenditures, and the scale cannot be determined from the outside.
For IonQ, at least until the first half of the year, the company's overall figures were almost entirely the figures for its quantum-related business (the SkyWater acquisition was at the end of July).
In the first half of this year (January to June), IonQ reduced its cash from its core business by about $250 million (outflow of operating cash flow). This is a threefold increase from the same period the previous year.
The cash Microsoft earns from its core business is about $500 million per day when divided by the number of days in a year. The cash IonQ burned over half a year is equivalent to about half a day's worth of that. Even when comparing the remainder after subtracting capital expenditures, it does not reach two days' worth.
It is unknown how much Microsoft actually spends on quantum. Even if we assume they were spending the same amount that IonQ burns in a year at its current pace, it would still only amount to about one day's worth of Microsoft's core business earnings. For IonQ, that amount represents the entire reduction in the company's cash.
The proportion of the budget determines the approach
Having worked in circuit design for over a decade, I feel that the way development proceeds is often determined more by the proportion of the total budget than by the amount of money itself.
In terms of circuit boards, the number of prototypes you can run is determined by how much the cost of that prototype accounts for the total budget. If a single prototype is small relative to the whole, you can build, measure, fix, and build again. You can also build two different proposals side-by-side and narrow it down to one after seeing the results. If a large part of the budget disappears in a single prototype, you spend much more time on verification before building, intending to get it right the first time.
A board intended to be completed in one go is also built differently. You include pads left empty without components, places where wiring can be switched later, and extra terminals for measurement. It is a method of building in backup paths on a single board so that if things don't go well, you can escape to another path without having to rebuild. Those who can run multiple prototypes don't have to go that far, as they can fix it in the next version.
Microsoft's quantum approach is closer to the former. Internally, they have chosen a method called topological qubits. It is a method that attempts to imbue the resistance of qubits to failure into the properties of the material itself, a path that almost no other major company has taken. Separately, they also announced in 2025 a plan to build an error-corrected quantum computer (Magne) for Denmark in collaboration with Atom Computing, which uses a different method called neutral atoms. On their own cloud (Azure Quantum), they also allow the use of machines from IonQ, Quantinuum, and Atom Computing. Even if their own method fails, if another company's method succeeds, they can continue to be involved as a partner or gateway (though the terms of their share are not public).
Research into the topological method has been long. Microsoft established its research center for this method in the mid-2000s, which is about 20 years ago now. In 2018, a paper by a group led by one of Microsoft's research heads (who was also a professor at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands) was published in Nature and retracted in 2021. Since then, they released their first chip (Majorana 1) in 2025 and the next chip (Majorana 2) in June of this year, and have set a goal to build a scalable quantum computer by 2029. Opinions among physicists are still divided as to whether a truly topological qubit has been created. In September, the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) became able to independently test the actual machine at Microsoft's facility. The results are yet to be published.
Even after the paper supporting their flagship method was retracted, they released a new chip four years later without changing the method. If the same thing had happened at a company specializing in quantum, I think the conditions for raising money next time would have changed significantly. This is a guess. A company that carries quantum with cash from its core business can wait without changing its method even if it stumbles.
“For as many years as it takes” cannot be verified from the outside
Even so, it cannot be said for certain that a company with a core business will continue to support quantum indefinitely.
As I wrote in a previous article, reports indicate that NEC stopped developing actual quantum computer hardware at the end of March 2026. Alibaba let go of its quantum laboratory in November 2023, and Baidu did the same in January 2024, despite both having core businesses.
In companies with a core business, quantum budgets are decided every year alongside other internal investment targets. In Microsoft's case, what sits next to it is the cloud and AI data centers, which account for the majority of capital expenditure. As long as quantum remains small and inconspicuous, it is less likely to be scrutinized in detail. Once it reaches the stage of scaling up machines toward the 2029 goal, the required amount will increase, and it will become visible within the company.
It is not as if there is no pressure to show results. Microsoft itself has explained that the 2029 goal is half of its original projection. The announcement of Majorana 1 received strong criticism from physicists.
The way things look when they are stopped is also different. Internal decisions are communicated externally only after they are finalized. NEC's withdrawal also came to light through reports rather than a company announcement. Since the quantum budget is not disclosed, it is difficult for Microsoft shareholders to read budget cuts from financial statements. IonQ is the opposite; how much cash has decreased and how many shares have been issued are released every quarter. Because it is visible, bad numbers immediately affect the stock price.
The weaknesses of IonQ pointed out in the article were indeed true when looking at the numbers.
A company that cannot generate its own funds until quantum becomes a business has no choice but to raise the shortfall from the market. In 2025 alone, IonQ raised over $3 billion through stock issuance. Some of this includes warrants that give the right to buy shares in the future at a fixed price. The purchase price is set higher than the current stock price, but if the stock price exceeds that level, these will be exercised, and the number of shares will increase by about 20% from now.
After using cash for the acquisition of SkyWater at the end of July, the cash on hand is said to be about $2 billion. Simply dividing this by the pace of the first half of the year, it is calculated to last about four years. This calculation does not include capital expenditure for SkyWater's factories or costs increased by the acquisition. The rate of cash burn has tripled in a year, and if it continues to increase at this rate, it will be even shorter.
With the acquisition of SkyWater, IonQ also gained revenue outside of quantum. This is contract manufacturing of semiconductors for defense, aerospace, and automotive industries. Of this year's revenue forecast, more than one-third is believed to be from SkyWater. Looking only at revenue, IonQ is no longer just a quantum company. However, SkyWater's gross margin (the percentage remaining after subtracting cost of goods sold from revenue) is around 20%, and it was in the red in the first half of 2026. The current numbers do not show cash from there supporting quantum research.
There is another way to look at it. Even if quantum fails, IonQ might remain as a company with factory and communication/sensor businesses. However, I don't think the current stock price reflects the value of those factories.
In Zacks' own ratings, IonQ was a 'Sell' and Microsoft was a 'Hold.' This rating is explained as an indicator for looking 1 to 3 months ahead, based on which way analysts' earnings estimates have been revised in the past few months. That is likely why the article title includes 'October.' In a comparison article of the same combination released by the same Zacks in May 2025, it was IonQ that was conversely considered to have large upside potential. The conclusion changes depending on the period, but the fact that losses continue and the stock price is high relative to revenue remains unchanged regardless of the period.
At this point, no one knows which method will perform useful calculations first. That said, there are factors in IonQ's favor. The company's focus is entirely on quantum, and there is no need to compete for budget with AI within the company. Microsoft's quantum revenue is not disclosed, but IonQ is already selling quantum computers, and its revenue is growing.
I think Microsoft can continue with quantum calmly because quantum is small within the company as a whole. Even if it fails, the company will not be shaken, and the impact on the stock price is diluted by the size of the core business. When it succeeds, it is diluted in the same way.
It seems that almost all of IonQ's stock price is riding on expectations for quantum.

IonQ stock jumps 12% following updated revenue outlook and SkyWater acquisition
The quantum computing company raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $450–460 million after closing its SkyWater Technology acquisition in July
IonQ’s stock surged roughly 12% on September 8, 2026, after the quantum computing company lifted its full-year revenue forecast and held its first-ever joint Investor Day. The catalyst was straightforward: a major acquisition that adds manufacturing muscle and, critically, meaningful revenue to the books.
The company raised its 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $450 million to $460 million, incorporating contributions from SkyWater Technology, a semiconductor foundry IonQ acquired on July 31, 2026. With the deal closing in late July, SkyWater accounts for roughly five months of consolidated revenue in the updated figures.
Before folding in SkyWater, IonQ’s standalone 2026 guidance already sat at $280 million to $290 million, itself a raise from earlier projections. The jump to $450–460 million reflects how transformative the SkyWater deal is to IonQ’s near-term revenue profile.
IonQ also reported that remaining performance obligations stood at $485 million at the end of Q2 2026. A backlog of that size signals customers are committing to future deliveries, which reduces the risk that current revenue growth is a one-time event.

IonQ vs. Rigetti: Is the Quantum Rally Backed by Fundamentals, or Just Momentum?
IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ) jumped roughly 12% in premarket trading on September 23 after testing the industry's first real-time quantum error decoder, then extended gains on reveals that its Superion quantum processor would be integrated into NVIDIA's Accelerated Quantum Research Center with Rigetti Computing, Inc. (NASDAQ:RGTI) trading up in sympathy on the same announcement, as the two stocks typically move together on sector-validating news. That said, a shared rally obscures a valuation gap between the two that's far wider than most sector-wide coverage lets on.
Curious to see how far Wall Street thinks the rally will go? BofA recently put a $60 price target on IonQ, here's the bull case in full.
IonQ's second-quarter revenue came in at $80 million, up 287% year-over-year, and management boosted its 2026 projection to $280-290 million, with combined revenue (after closing the SkyWater foundry purchase) potentially reaching $460 million for the year. The company had roughly $2 billion in pro-forma cash, cash equivalents and investments following the SkyWater acquisition, dwarfing Rigetti's approximately $540 million, giving IonQ significantly more runway to fund years of pre-commercial R&D without fear of dilution.
On the tech front, IonQ's trapped-ion design appears to have an accuracy advantage in recent comparisons, with IonQ reporting strong two-qubit gate-fidelity results, although direct comparisons with Rigetti are not straightforward. However, Rigetti's architecture offers an advantage in terms of speed. The distinction is significant because quantum computing is not a simple race in which one company is "ahead" on every metric: accuracy, gate speed, scalability, connectivity, and error correction are all important. IonQ's advantage is thus best regarded as a technical and financial one, rather than proof that it has already won the architecture race. Rigetti remains open to the potential that advancements in speed, production, or error correction could close the gap.
The valuation gap gets flattened when these two stocks are discussed together. IonQ's market capitalization is currently around $17.48 billion, compared to combined 2026 revenue guidance of $450 million to $460 million following the SkyWater acquisition, putting its forward price-to-sales multiple in the 39x range. This is already a notable multiple, but it is built on a path to nearly triple-digit revenue growth and a roughly $2 billion of pro-forma cash, cash equivalents and investments that reduces near-term funding risk.
Meanwhile, Rigetti, with a market capitalization that has fluctuated between $5 billion to $9 billion over the last year, trades at an unusual trailing price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 391.65x, having previously reached nearly 1,000x during substantial trading spikes.
While trailing multiples for both businesses remain elevated due to small historical sales bases, the valuation gap remains substantial. Simply put, the market is charging investors much more per dollar of current revenue for Rigetti than for IonQ, despite IonQ having a far stronger balance sheet and a larger revenue base.
That disparity becomes significant because it signals potential downside risk if sentiment cools. A stock trading at 39x forward sales has priced in high growth, while a stock trading at several hundred times trailing sales has priced in near-perfect execution over a much longer time horizon, with far less revenue currently on the books to anchor that multiple if the growth narrative stalls even briefly.
Insider selling adds another cautious signal to the group. Since September 2024, insiders at IonQ, Rigetti, D-Wave, and Quantum Computing Inc. have collectively sold around $895.1 million more stock than they bought. On September 11, IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi sold 16,121 shares for around $598,000, though the filing said that the transaction was non-discretionary and was used to meet tax obligations related to vested restricted stock units.
Hedge fund positioning has grown for both companies, although Rigetti Computing, Inc. (NASDAQ:RGTI) has seen a greater gain. The number of hedge funds owning IonQ, Inc. (NYSE:IONQ) jumped from 39 in the first quarter to 42 in the second, while Rigetti's ownership increased from 29 to 34 funds. That suggests that institutional investors are increasing exposure to the quantum theme rather than focusing solely on the better-capitalized leader. The short-interest numbers reflect a far wider contrast over Rigetti: short interest is 10.15% of IonQ's shares versus 19.07% for Rigetti.
Neither stock is a value investment, since both remain speculative bets on a technology that is still years away from widespread commercial application. However, the valuation math argues for treating them very differently within that assumption. IonQ's multiple, while extreme by any conventional measure, is supported by a larger revenue base, faster reported growth, and a cash position that provides years of runway without dilution risk. Rigetti's multiple requires investors to pay several times more per dollar of current sales for a company with a fraction of the cash cushion, implying that any slowdown in its growth rate or the need to raise capital would cause the stock to fall from a far less defensible valuation baseline. Investors drawn to the sector by names like these should treat the price-to-sales gap, not just the shared NVIDIA headline, as the more important number, and should keep an eye on upcoming quarters to see if Rigetti's own revenue growth can actually close that multiple gap, or if the current premium is simply compensation that the market hasn't yet demanded fully.

IonQ Takes Quantum Computing to NVIDIA's Research Center: What's Next?
Zacks Investment Research - Zacks Investment Research - Mon Sep 28, 9:14AM CDT
IonQ IONQ is set to become the first company to deploy an on-premise quantum computing system at NVIDIA’sAccelerated Quantum Research Center (“NVAQC”). The facility is designed to address key challenges in scaling quantum processors into a new class of accelerated quantum supercomputers.
IonQ’s full-stack quantum systems will be connected directly to NVIDIA’s AI infrastructure to advance qubits into useful, large-scale quantum supercomputers. The integration is expected to help tackle some of the world’s complex problems. Under the partnership, IonQ’s Superion 256 system will be installed at NVAQC and linked directly to NVIDIA’s GB200 NVL72 system through NVQLink. The workloads will be orchestrated through NVIDIA’s open CUDA-Q platform. The joint research effort will center on hybrid software development and large-scale system prototyping, producing open results and guidance for future AI applications and quantum-GPU co-design.
Superion 256 was introduced earlier this month and is the first in the Superion platform that all future compute products are expected to be built on. The platform scales from 256 qubits to millions of qubits, with every generation that follows Superion 256 expanding use of the same ions, the same qubits, the same electronic control and the same chip fabric. Installation at NVAQC is scheduled for next year.
Alongside quantum-GPU integration, joint research is expected to target quantum algorithms portfolio optimization and risk modeling in financial services, materials science and computational chemistry for drug discovery. These types of complex use cases will benefit from research conducted using the Superion 256 system.
IonQ and NVIDIA recently joined Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the University of Tennessee on research aimed at addressing complex combinatorial optimization problems. Presented at IEEE Quantum Week earlier this month, the award-winning study paired generative AI with distributed quantum algorithms and ran on NVIDIA’s CUDA-Q platform.
Quantinuum QNT is building the technology and supply-chain foundation needed to scale fault-tolerant systems, together with its domestic partners. The company has recently finalized an agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce’s CHIPS Research and Development Office for $100 million in federal funding under the CHIPS and Science Act. The award follows a letter of intent announced in May and will support R&D and U.S.-based quantum semiconductor manufacturing capabilities needed to deploy large-scale, fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computers.
Besides, GlobalFoundries GFS, or GF, will be one of several of Quantinuum's foundries enlisted to fabricate its next-generation ion traps and other electronics, specifically focused on using 300mm wafer technology. The company has continued to advance its quantum technology roadmap and deepen collaborations across the quantum ecosystem. GF also announced that it has finalized a definitive agreement for a $375 million CHIPS award to accelerate its Quantum Technology Solutions business.
Over the past 12 months, IonQ shares have dropped 29.2% compared to the industry’s 210.9% growth.
In terms of valuation, IONQ trades at a forward, five-year price-to-sales (P/S) of 23.72X compared with the 5.35X industry average.

Quantum computing has a huge market opportunity that's quickly approaching. Many in the industry now project 2029 as the year viable quantum computing technology arrives, which isn't all that far away. Companies of all sizes are vying for viable quantum computing technology, including some of the largest in the world. At the same time, several upstarts are attempting to capture market share, and this new technology has the potential to create several incredible new companies.
One of the brightest quantum computing upstarts is IonQ (IONQ -1.83%). IonQ is taking a different approach to quantum computing than its peers, and it's looking very promising. Another major competitor is Alphabet (GOOG +1.02%) (GOOGL +0.86%), the world's third-largest company.
These two are completely different sizes and have different return levels, but which is the better investment?
Image source: Getty Images.
There are multiple pathways for quantum computing
Quantum computing is more of a concept than an established technique. The general idea is to use a particle's movements to perform calculations, but how that particle is controlled varies from company to company. Companies are trying different approaches to best control particles for calculations, ranging from superconducting computing (like Alphabet) to trapped ion (IonQ). Each approach has its own strengths and weaknesses, but it ultimately boils down to two factors: speed and accuracy.
Alphabet is taking an approach that optimizes speed over accuracy. The idea here is that, eventually, the technology will become accurate enough that faster processing speeds will be more attractive to clients.

IonQ's approach optimizes for accuracy and is working on processing speed by adding more qubits, the quantum computing equivalent of bits. While its approach may be slower, sheer size can make up for it.
Nobody knows which technique will ultimately win, so investing in companies with a variety of approaches makes the most sense. However, one company has much more to gain than the other.
With IonQ's only business being quantum computing, it must produce a viable product or go bankrupt. While that life-or-death comparison may seem a bit stark, it's the reality for an upstart like IonQ. Fortunately, it has several partners and is nearing production of its 256-qubit system, which could be the first viable early-stage quantum computing product ever released.
If that product sees strong adoption, the market may get on board with IonQ's prospects and send its stock skyrocketing. Since it's a relatively small $16 billion company, it wouldn't take much of a boost to send its stock skyrocketing. Alphabet is different. If its quantum computing product lineup doesn't pan out and goes bust, the stock really wouldn't be affected. It would still proceed with its normal plan to produce incredible AI products and dominate the online search industry. While it may have missed an opportunity to provide leading quantum computing units for its cloud computing business, it will still be a strong investment.
Even if it does develop a viable quantum computing product, there are questions as to how much it will actually affect Alphabet's financial picture. During the second quarter, Alphabet generated nearly $120 billion in revenue.
An additional $1 billion in revenue doesn't really move the needle for Alphabet. However, it would mean the world to IonQ and its shareholders.
So, if you're looking for ultimate upside, but with high risk, IonQ is the better quantum computing stock pick. However, if you're looking for guaranteed positive returns and little risk with some quantum computing exposure, Alphabet is the better stock pick of the two.

IonQ (NYSE:IONQ | IONQ Price Prediction) currently trades at $43.87. Wall Street’s average price target is $66.63, which implies 51.9% upside.
IonQ is a pure-play quantum computing company. It sells trapped-ion systems along with quantum networking, sensing and security products. It just posted its fifth consecutive record quarter and raised full-year revenue guidance to $280 million to $290 million. Two sell-side firms, B. Riley Securities and Rosenblatt Securities, share a Street-high target of $100.00. That target implies 127.9% upside.
That gap suggests either the market or the analysts have misjudged IonQ.
Losses, Dilution and a Sector Selloff Cut IonQ Nearly in Half From Its High
Losses caused the decline. Q2 revenue reached $80.05M, up 286.8%. Yet adjusted EBITDA loss came to $120.3 million and GAAP net loss hit $1.87B. A $1.6B warrant fair-value charge caused most of that loss; stock-based compensation added $141.8M. A $2B equity offering diluted existing shareholders.
Shares are down 28.67% over 12 months and sit 48.2% below the 52-week high of $84.64.
The sector sold off widely. IonQ’s fiscal 2027 consensus EPS estimate fell from -$2.3667 90 days ago to -$3.3720.
Eleven of 13 Analysts Still Rate IonQ a Buy
Of the 13 analysts tracked, one rates IonQ a Strong Buy, 10 rate it a Buy, two rate it a Hold and none rate it a Sell. The latest move was a new initiation: Bank of America started covering the stock with a Buy rating.
Three drivers support the $100 bull case: trapped-ion technology scaling toward error-corrected systems, bookings from multi-year quantum-as-a-service contracts with hyperscalers and defense agencies, and a path to $1B in annualized revenue run-rates. Consensus fiscal 2027 revenue is about $811 million.
Backlog supports this. Remaining performance obligations reached $485 million, up from $122 million a year earlier. Catalysts include commissioning 256-qubit systems in the first half of next year and moving toward 10,000 qubits in 2027. The Anduril and Sandia agreements are not included in backlog or guidance, so revenue from them would be upside.
Price targets carry no guarantee. Most of the thesis depends on hardware milestones arriving in 2027.
Rigetti and D-Wave Fell Harder, and Their Targets Imply More Upside
All three quantum stocks sold off together. IonQ held up best.
Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) is down 47.16% over one year. It trades at $15.74 against a $28.52 target, which implies 81.2% upside. Nine of 13 analysts rate it Buy or Strong Buy and four say Hold. Q2 revenue was only $5.14 million.
D-Wave Quantum (NYSE:QBTS) is down 32.94% over one year. At $16.57 against a $34.65 target, it implies 109.1% upside. Sixteen of 17 analysts rate it a Buy or better, even though Q2 revenue of $3.08 million missed estimates.
D-Wave has the most analyst-implied upside. IonQ has the least, but it generates far more revenue than either peer, so its upside rests on reported sales.
IonQ Trailed the S&P 500 by a Wide Margin Over the Past Year
IonQ trades at $43.87. The average target from 13 analysts is $66.63, or 51.9% upside. Over the past year, the stock fell 28.67% while the S&P 500 gained 14.46%. Year to date, IonQ is down 2.23% and the index is up 11.81%.
Short-term momentum is stronger. IonQ rose 11.6% over the past month while the S&P 500 fell 0.6%. Beta is 3.295, the 52-week low is $25.89, and shares trade at 72 times trailing sales.
IonQ’s Sales Growth Faces a Test From Widening Losses
This outlook improves if the 256-qubit systems launch on schedule, combined guidance with SkyWater Technology (NASDAQ:SKYT) shows revenue growing faster than costs, and backlog turns to sales. That path supports the $66.63 consensus target.
The bear case improves if adjusted EBITDA losses grow, more equity raises dilute shareholders, or acquisition integration stalls. At 72 times sales, execution slips leave little margin.
IonQ is the only company in this group with real revenue scale, making its smaller upside the most credible. The $100 target needs everything right. The consensus target needs steady execution.

IonQ's 2027 Revenue Math Meets a Market That Won't Wait Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Quantum computing has long been sold as the next frontier of technology, a realm where qubits unlock problems that classical machines can only stare at in frustration. IonQ sits squarely at the center of that promise — and squarely in the uncomfortable gap between laboratory breakthroughs and the revenue lines investors actually care about.
That tension was on full display Monday, when the stock slipped 0.8% to close at EUR 38.32 even as the broader market moved higher. With no company-specific bad news to point to, observers attributed the pullback to profit-taking and the stock's persistently wide trading range. The shares remain 48% below their 52-week high, a discount that says plenty about how much skepticism still surrounds the young sector's high-growth pioneers.
Wall Street Sees the Story, Just Not Yet the Earnings
Mizuho Securities offered a counterweight the same day, reaffirming its "Outperform" rating with a $52.00 price target after meetings with IonQ's CFO and COO. The analysts acknowledged prior target cuts tied to valuation concerns following the company's analyst day, but left the quantum growth narrative intact. Their confidence leans heavily on 2027, when the ramp-up of Superion 256 systems is expected to take hold.
Bank of America Securities had already planted its flag a few days earlier, initiating coverage on September 28 with a Buy rating and a $60.00 target. The bank pointed to semiconductor-based scaling and IonQ's broad positioning across quantum computing, communication, and sensing as the pillars of its thesis.
The order book looks impressive on paper. Mizuho estimates Superion 256 systems could sell for $25 million to $30 million apiece — meaningful sums that could reshape the company's financial base. The catch is timing. IonQ announced a contract with Florida International University on September 24 to deliver a Superion 256, but campus installation isn't slated until late 2027. A separate, higher-profile project near Nvidia — announced roughly two weeks ago — follows the same 2027 timeline, though the stock has gained 2.5% since that disclosure.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying IonQ?
Investors, in other words, are being asked to bridge a multi-year gap between signed agreements and recognized revenue.
The scientific progress is harder to dismiss. On September 22, IonQ's team demonstrated a real-time quantum error-correction decoder running on a standard commercial processor. Benchmark circuits simulated up to 408 logical qubits and more than 31.5 million operations with minimal stretching time — a direct strike at one of the biggest bottlenecks on the road to fault-tolerant computing.
Two days later, the company reported a generative quantum model for radar applications that outperformed two classical comparison methods. In one test case, the system posted a filtered F1 score of 0.41 against classical baselines of 0.24 and 0.16. The study also exposed a limitation: when raw data were preprocessed to approximate a Gaussian distribution, the quantum advantage largely evaporated.
IonQ has kept its commercial outreach running alongside the research. On October 1, it launched the CQ Connect webinar series with EPB, aimed at showing executives how to apply quantum and networking technology in practice.
Technically, the stock is holding a modest line. At EUR 38.32, it trades just above its 200-day moving average of EUR 37.70 — a thin cushion given the 48% gap to its 52-week high.
The setup captures IonQ's core dilemma: ambitious plans that demand years of investor faith before the numbers arrive. Buying this stock isn't buying an established business — it's a wager on flawless scaling through 2027. Any delay along that path would likely hit the shares hard. The technological case is real, and the partnerships with heavyweights and research institutions keep IonQ visible and validated. But until commercial viability catches up with the vision, valuation anxiety will set the tempo.

I Calculated IonQ's Gross Margin Myself: A Hardware Engineer's Two-Part Take on 'Scaling Makes It Cheaper'
On September 29, the U.S. investment news site Motley Fool published a short article titled 'IonQ Stock Looks Expensive. Can Scale Justify It?' According to another article on the same site, the stock price is about 50 times its revenue. The article cites 'manufacturing efficiency' as one of the conditions to justify this. It does not specify what that refers to (the main body of the article is a video, which I have not watched).
From the perspective of someone who has been designing circuits for over a decade, the phrase 'it gets cheaper as volume increases' conflates two different things. Looking back at IonQ's financial statements, their gross margin has actually decreased while their revenue has quadrupled over the past year.
Hardware costs should be thought of in two broad categories.
The first is development costs, which are paid only once. This includes design, verification, masks for chips (the master plates used to print circuit patterns), inspection jigs (specialized tools for holding or measuring products), programs, and reliability testing. In the industry, this is called NRE (Non-Recurring Engineering). Whether you make 10 units or 10,000, you generally only pay this once.
The second is the cost incurred every time you build a single unit. This includes parts, assembly, adjustment, inspection time, and the portion discarded due to defects.
It is the former that automatically dilutes as the number of units increases. If you divide the development costs by the number of units, the burden per unit becomes smaller.
The latter does not work that way. If the adjustment process—where you connect measuring instruments and align the output for each unit one by one during prototyping—remains, the effort required for one unit will hardly change whether it is the 10th unit or the 100th. Reviewing the design before mass production is done to reduce this. By reducing the number of adjustment points and establishing jigs and procedures, you ensure that anyone can achieve the same result. Products that have not undergone this process will remain expensive per unit even if the volume increases.
Replaced with an investor's perspective, these two appear on different lines of the financial statement. Most development costs go into R&D expenses, while the cost per unit goes into the cost of goods sold (COGS). If the former is diluted, 'R&D expenses ÷ revenue' decreases. If the latter decreases, the gross margin (the percentage of revenue remaining after subtracting the cost of goods sold) increases. Both are sometimes called 'scaling,' but you look at different places.
IonQ's financial statements do not always fit this classification perfectly. In contracts for equipment built for customers, the labor costs for the design of that equipment are also included in the cost of goods sold. I will touch on the treatment of machines held by the company itself later.
Quantum computer components are divided into those that easily become cheaper through mass production and those that do not
IonQ's next machine, the Superion 256, centers on a chip. According to the explanation from Oxford Ionics, which IonQ acquired, the electrodes that levitate the ions and the antennas that manipulate the qubits are built into a single silicon chip. IonQ calls this method EQC (Electronic Qubit Control). Its selling point is that it can be manufactured using standard semiconductor processes.
Chips are the components where the effects of mass production are most effective. You can get many from a single wafer, and as the process stabilizes, defects also decrease.
What about the outside of the chip? Oxford Ionics writes that for their machines, server racks are lined up outside the vacuum chamber, containing the lasers used for qubit preparation and readout, as well as the electronic circuits that send signals to the chip. Even if qubit manipulation is moved from lasers to electronic control, the lasers for preparation and readout remain.
From here on, it is speculation. I see the lasers, optical components, vacuum chambers, cooling systems, and the work of assembling and adjusting them as less susceptible to the effects of mass production than the chip. The effort to align light positions, create a vacuum, and adjust everything until it works for each unit does not decrease significantly at the stage of a few to several dozen units. If the control electronic circuits are built with commercially available semiconductor parts, they would likely fall somewhere in between.
Lined up this way, one can also read the reason why IonQ is prioritizing integration into the chip. It appears they are trying to shift as many functions as possible to the side that becomes cheaper through mass production. In the next generation, the Superion 10K, they plan to include even the CMOS control circuits (standard semiconductor chip circuits) on the chip.
IonQ expects that by moving from lasers to semiconductor-based control, they can reduce the cost per qubit by more than 300 times across their entire roadmap. One must be careful how to read this figure. If the number of qubits on a chip increases, the cost per qubit will decrease even if the surrounding equipment remains almost the same. Oxford Ionics also writes that even if the chip is made larger, the surrounding equipment hardly needs to change. What appears directly in the gross margin is how much one unit is sold for and how much one unit cost. Even if the figure per qubit goes down, it does not necessarily mean the cost per unit goes down.
The story of parts costs follows the same pattern. At an analyst briefing in September 2025, IonQ presented an external estimate that the parts cost (BOM, total bill of materials) for one machine could be kept quite low. However, this applies to large machines several generations ahead, not the machines currently being sold. Only parts costs go into the bill of materials. Labor costs for assembly and adjustment, and the portion discarded due to defects, are additional costs.
Regarding current costs, there is an explanation in the quarterly report (10-Q). As the main reason for the increase in the cost of goods sold in the April-June quarter, they cite an increase in labor costs to fulfill contracts, along with an increase in material costs for quantum products. It is unclear whether the labor costs are for assembly work or for design and service personnel. Labor costs also include stock-based compensation, and about one-fourth of the increase in costs was due to this.
Previously, after reading the announcement of the Superion 256, I wrote about thinking of the chip layer and the finished machine layer separately.
In this installment, I will continue by applying these two layers of costs to the lines in the financial statements.
Restarting yield ramp-up with every new generation
Superion 256 is a new generation of chip. It has been announced that six tape-outs (passing design data to the factory for manufacturing) were completed in the first half of 2026, and that ions have been successfully trapped in prototypes. Orders are already being accepted, with customer deliveries scheduled for 2027.
For a new generation of chip, it is normal for the initial yield (the percentage of usable items among those produced) to be low. Each time a lot (a batch of units sent through the factory) is processed, the source of defects is investigated, and either the process or the design is corrected. Through this repetition, the percentage increases, and the cost per unit stabilizes. From a design perspective, the day a new product is announced corresponds to standing at the bottom of this long slope.
There are also factors favorable to IonQ. According to IonQ, the number of wafer lots processed in collaboration with SkyWater, the semiconductor factory whose acquisition was completed at the end of July, was 12 times higher in a six-month period compared to the previous contract manufacturer. The time required for one design cycle has also reportedly shrunk from nine months to two months. Processing more lots increases the opportunities to investigate the causes of defects. This speed could become a strength.
What concerns me is the short interval until the next generation arrives. For Superion 10K, there is a goal to achieve error correction (the ability to continue operating while fixing calculation errors) in a laboratory setting in 2027 and to commercialize it in 2028. The delivery period for the 256 and the launch of the next generation overlap significantly. Generally speaking, if you add CMOS circuits to a chip, the number of processes increases, and the probability of a defect occurring somewhere on a single chip also rises.
If you manufacture using the same factory and the same processes, the causes of defects found in the previous generation can be carried over to the next. IonQ also notes that the technology for incorporating CMOS is already being mass-produced by SkyWater. Even so, if the trend of moving to the next generation continues before the yield of a single generation has fully matured, the cost per unit will continue to fluctuate without ever stabilizing for any generation.
Regarding this point, IonQ explains that because future generations will be designed, manufactured, and packaged in the same way, the machinery can be upgraded. If chips can be swapped out and the surrounding equipment reused, the development costs incurred for the surrounding infrastructure will be diluted across generations. Once the first machines are installed at customer sites, it will become clear to what extent they can actually be reused.
The first few units often require more effort than estimated. IonQ recognizes revenue for customer-bound equipment not when it is completed and delivered, but gradually in line with the progress of the costs incurred to build it (accounting policy in the 10-Q). With this method, any costs that exceed the plan act to push down the gross margin. The figures for individual contracts are not disclosed. I am writing this as a speculation based on the accounting mechanism.
What can be verified from the outside, and what cannot
I calculated the gross margin myself from the figures in the financial statements (using figures before deducting depreciation, in line with IonQ's disclosures). For the April-June quarter, it was approximately 25%, a significant drop from approximately 60% in the same period of the previous year. While that quarter of the previous year was on the high side, the downward trend remained the same even when viewed on an annual basis.
The cost of goods sold includes stock-based compensation. Even if you calculate excluding that, it has fallen from nearly 70% to the 40% range.
Research and development expenses appear to be diluted. In the April-June quarter of the previous year, they were about five times the revenue, while this year they are about twice the revenue. Most of this shrinkage comes from a decrease in stock-based compensation included in R&D expenses. Excluding stock-based compensation, the ratio to revenue has hardly moved. R&D expenses themselves are increasing at almost the same rate as revenue.
Regarding the reason for the decline in gross margin, the company has not touched upon the contents of the cost of goods sold. At the May earnings call, when asked about the decline in gross margin for the January-March quarter, COO and CFO Mr. Singh replied: This industry is still in its infancy, and scale will grow over time. We certainly prioritize gross margin. As revenue doubles, we will be able to address the cost of goods sold. Right now, it changes depending on what we sold more of in that quarter. What is IONQ? The NVIDIA of the quantum world
In the quantum computer industry, multiple companies such as IBM, Google, Quantinuum, and IonQ are continuing a development race using different methods, and at present, there is no overwhelming winner like NVIDIA in generative AI.
Among them, what makes IonQ significantly different from other companies is that it does not just compete on the performance of the quantum computer itself, but consolidates the manufacturing of quantum chips, quantum networks, quantum security, quantum sensing, and satellite communications into a single corporate group, and is attempting to become a company that supplies technology to the entire quantum industry.
From 2025 to 2026, IonQ successively acquired Oxford Ionics, Lightsynq, ID Quantique, and Capella Space, and in July 2026, it completed the acquisition of the US semiconductor foundry SkyWater Technology. Furthermore, in September, it announced the next-generation quantum computer "Superion 256," which uses chips manufactured at SkyWater, and immediately after, it was decided that the system would be introduced to NVIDIA's quantum research base.
Looking at this series of moves, what IonQ is aiming for is not just a quantum computer manufacturer.
What the company is aiming for is a "quantum platform company" that handles everything from designing quantum computers, manufacturing them in semiconductor factories, connecting them via quantum networks, combining them with clouds and supercomputers, and selling them to governments and companies, all within one company.
1 IonQ's characteristic lies in the "ion trap" type
There is no single common manufacturing method for quantum computers, and each company creates qubits using different methods.
While IBM and Google adopt the superconducting method, IonQ and Quantinuum adopt the ion trap method, which captures ions in the air using electromagnetic fields and uses their internal states as qubits.
The feature of the ion trap method is that it is easy to increase the quality of qubits and easy to directly manipulate distant qubits. IonQ announced in 2025 that it had achieved 99.99% fidelity in a 2-qubit gate, making high-precision quantum manipulation one of the company's technical strengths.
On the other hand, the ion trap method also has challenges. Compared to the superconducting method, gate operations tend to be slower, and how to scale from the stage of handling dozens or hundreds of ions to tens or hundreds of thousands of qubits becomes a major problem.
Therefore, what is important when considering IonQ's long-term competitiveness is not the current number of qubits itself.
The biggest point is whether it can transition to a structure that can be mass-produced using semiconductor manufacturing technology while maintaining the advantage of the ion trap method, which is high precision.
2 By acquiring Oxford Ionics, quantum computers have been brought closer to "semiconductors"
An important move by IonQ to address this problem is the UK-based Oxford Ionics, which it acquired in 2025 for approximately $1.075 billion.
Oxford Ionics also adopts the same ion trap method as IonQ, but a major feature is that it has the technology to replace part of the complex laser equipment for controlling qubits with electronic circuits on a semiconductor chip.
IonQ completed the acquisition of Oxford Ionics in September 2025 and indicated a policy of integrating the company's semiconductor-based quantum control technology into IonQ's quantum computers.
What this acquisition means is that IonQ is trying to change quantum computers from special devices assembled one by one in a laboratory into products that can be mass-produced using the manufacturing methods of the semiconductor industry.
And it was the acquisition of SkyWater that took this strategy one step further.
3 The SkyWater acquisition is not just about sales expansion for IonQ
In January 2026, IonQ announced the acquisition of U.S. semiconductor foundry SkyWater Technology for approximately $1.8 billion, completing the deal on July 31. SkyWater is a foundry with semiconductor manufacturing facilities within the United States, and following the acquisition, it will continue to manufacture semiconductors for customers other than IonQ while also taking on the production of IonQ's quantum chips.
The significance of a quantum computer company owning a semiconductor foundry itself is immense.
Typically, when a quantum computer company develops a new chip, it must repeat a cycle of requesting manufacturing from an external semiconductor maker, receiving prototypes, evaluating them, revising the design, and requesting manufacturing again.
By bringing SkyWater into its corporate group, IonQ will be able to closely integrate everything from quantum chip design to prototyping, manufacturing, and packaging in-house.
This is not merely an acquisition to lower manufacturing costs.
Improving quantum computer performance is not a one-time task of completing a chip; it requires repeating design changes and manufacturing at high speed many times, so by directly owning a foundry, there is a possibility of shortening the development cycle itself.
At the time of the acquisition announcement, IonQ indicated plans to begin functional testing of a QPU with 200,000 physical qubits and approximately 8,000 logical qubits in 2028, and to accelerate the development timeline for a 2-million-qubit chip by up to one year. While these are the company's own roadmap goals and not yet achieved figures, it is clear that the purpose of the SkyWater acquisition is not to increase current revenue, but to secure a manufacturing foundation for scaling up to tens of thousands or millions of qubits.
4 The answer to that is the "Superion 256" announced in September
Following the SkyWater acquisition, IonQ announced its 6th-generation quantum computer, the "Superion 256," on September 8, 2026.
The Superion 256 is a system equipped with 256 physical qubits and is the first major product to combine the electronic control technology acquired from Oxford Ionics with SkyWater's semiconductor manufacturing capabilities.
What is noteworthy is that the first chips have already been manufactured at SkyWater, and the prototype system has successfully trapped ions. IonQ began accepting orders as of September 2026 and plans to deliver to the first customers in 2027.
In other words, the acquisitions of Oxford Ionics and SkyWater are not just future concepts; they are already being reflected in next-generation products.
The biggest point to watch for IonQ over the next few years is whether it can actually scale from 256 qubits to thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of thousands of qubits using this Superion architecture.
5 NVIDIA introduces IonQ to its quantum research center
One of the most important pieces of recent news for IonQ is the partnership with NVIDIA announced on September 23, 2026.
At the "NVIDIA Accelerated Quantum Research Center," which researches the integration of quantum computing and GPU supercomputing, it has been decided that IonQ's Superion 256 will be introduced as the first on-premises quantum processor.
The Superion 256 will be directly connected to NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 via NVQLink, creating a configuration that utilizes GPUs and quantum processors in an integrated manner through CUDA-Q.
This partnership is important because it is highly likely that future quantum computers will not completely replace current supercomputers.
In reality, it is considered highly likely that we will see a "hybrid" computing environment where CPUs, GPUs, and QPUs each handle the calculations they are best at: normal processing for CPUs, large-scale parallel computing and AI for GPUs, and only the parts where quantum mechanical processing has an advantage passed to the QPU.
In that case, what becomes important for quantum computer companies is not just competing on QPU performance alone, but whether they can integrate their own QPUs into NVIDIA GPUs and existing supercomputers.
The introduction of IonQ's Superion as the first QPU at an NVIDIA research facility holds significant meaning beyond the scale of commercial revenue, particularly when considering IonQ's position within this hybrid computing environment.
6. Recent financial results show revenue growth at a speed unusual for a quantum company
While looking solely at IonQ's technological development might make it seem like a story for the future, its revenue growth has recently become rapid.
Revenue for the April-June 2026 quarter reached $80.1 million, a 287% increase from approximately $20.7 million in the same period last year. Cumulative revenue for January-June 2026 is approximately $144.7 million, already surpassing the $130 million in revenue for the full year of 2025 in just six months.
The composition of revenue is also changing.
In the second quarter, approximately 60% came from commercial customers such as private companies, and about 50% came from sales outside the U.S., with revenue from customers purchasing multiple IonQ products accounting for about 25%. IonQ is moving beyond the stage of relying solely on U.S. government research contracts and is expanding its customer base to include corporations, universities, and foreign governments.
Furthermore, Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO), which indicate contracts to be recognized as future revenue, have increased by 297% year-over-year, meaning that not only current recognized revenue but also contracted projects are expanding.
The revenue outlook for 2026 has also been revised upward multiple times.
The annual revenue forecast, which was $225 million to $245 million as of February 2026, was raised to $260 million to $270 million in May, and to $280 million to $290 million in August. Furthermore, on September 8, following the SkyWater acquisition, the annual revenue forecast was raised to $450 million to $460 million by consolidating SkyWater's revenue from July 31 onwards.
However, caution is required here.
The majority of the increase from $290 million to nearly $460 million is not the result of a sudden surge in IonQ's core quantum business, but rather the result of consolidating SkyWater.
Therefore, when looking at IonQ going forward, it is necessary to check not only the consolidated revenue but also the organic growth rate of the quantum business excluding SkyWater separately.
7. Revenue is growing rapidly, but it is currently still significantly in the red
On the other hand, IonQ is not currently a mature company that generates profit.
Adjusted EBITDA for the second quarter of 2026 was a loss of $120.3 million, and even excluding costs associated with the SkyWater transaction, it was a loss of $95.6 million. Research and development expenses alone reached $160.6 million, an amount significantly exceeding the $80.1 million in quarterly revenue invested into R&D.
The GAAP-based net loss appears very large at approximately $1.868 billion, but this figure includes a loss of approximately $1.649 billion due to changes in the fair value of warrant liabilities, so not all of it is cash outflow from business operations. When looking at the reality of the business, it is necessary to look at adjusted EBITDA and cash balances, not just net loss.
As of the end of June, the company held approximately $3 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and investment securities, and it states that approximately $2 billion will remain even on a pro-forma basis reflecting the cash used for the SkyWater acquisition.
In other words, IonQ is currently in a stage of continuing to make upfront investments in quantum computers, networks, sensing, and semiconductor manufacturing while posting significant losses. While it has sufficient funds for future growth, the question is whether it can truly commercialize large-scale quantum systems using those funds.
8. IonQ is not just acquiring quantum computers
What is important in understanding IonQ's strategy is

The search for explosive growth often leads investors to IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and SoundHound AI (SOUN +0.69%). Each company is pioneering a different frontier of the modern technological landscape to capture market share.
IonQ specializes in the complex world of quantum hardware, while SoundHound AI focuses on conversational artificial intelligence. Both represent high-risk, high-reward opportunities for those interested in emerging technologies. This comparison explores which business model and financial profile offer a more compelling path forward for retail investors.
IonQ develops trapped-ion quantum computing, quantum networking, sensing, and security solutions. In its latest annual report, the company details how it offers Quantum-Computing-as-a-Service through major cloud providers like Amazon (AMZN -0.05%) and Microsoft (MSFT +1.48%). It also maintains a presence on the Google Cloud Marketplace. As IonQ advances its footprint in the tech stocks landscape, it recently acquired SkyWater Technology to establish an internal secure quantum foundry. This move helps the company manage its own supply chain and hardware development.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $130.0 million, which is a significant increase from roughly $43.1 million in the prior year. This represents revenue growth of approximately 201.9% as the company scales its commercial operations. However, the company reported a net loss of nearly $510.4 million for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of close to -392.6%. The company continues to spend heavily on research and development to maintain its technological edge.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x. This means the company carries no debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at roughly 15.5x, which indicates that IonQ has many more current assets than current liabilities. Free cash flow for the period was negative $299.6 million, as the company prioritized building out its hardware infrastructure. Free cash flow is calculated by subtracting capital expenditures from cash provided by operations.
SoundHound AI delivers voice and agentic AI software that delivers conversational experiences across various industries. These include the automotive, hospitality, and retail sectors where voice interaction is becoming a standard feature. In late 2026, the company completed the acquisition of LivePerson to expand its enterprise AI and omnichannel customer engagement capabilities. The company integrates its platform with existing third-party telecommunications and internet infrastructure to serve enterprise customers. Its technology is found in everything from smart devices and televisions to in-vehicle systems.
In FY 2025, revenue was close to $168.9 million, representing a 99.4% jump from the approximately $84.7 million reported in 2024. Despite this rapid growth, the company reported a net loss of nearly $14.0 million. This reflects a net margin of approximately -8.3% for the fiscal year. This margin is a significant improvement from the much larger losses reported in previous fiscal periods. The company is working toward achieving profitability as it expands its footprint in the voice AI market.
According to its December 2025 balance sheet, SoundHound AI has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x. The current ratio, which measures the company's ability to cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, is roughly 4.6x. Free cash flow was negative $103.1 million for the year. This figure is determined by taking cash from operations and subtracting capital expenditures. The company continues to invest in its agentic AI platform to stay ahead of evolving consumer demands.
IonQ faces risks from the unproven nature of scalable quantum computing. It relies heavily on specialized personnel and faces complex international regulatory laws. Significant historical losses require the company to potentially seek more capital.
SoundHound AI deals with high customer concentration and intense competition from companies like Nvidia (NVDA +2.12%). It has also disclosed material weaknesses in internal controls over financial reporting. There are also legal risks regarding the accuracy of its generative AI tools.
SoundHound AI is cheaper based on its P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with IonQ, though this is a speculative pick that comes with real caveats. Both companies are early-stage and unprofitable, and IonQ's losses are substantial, as it is burning through cash at a significant pace to achieve its current scale.
IonQ's revenue guidance jumped dramatically this year, though much of that increase reflects the SkyWater acquisition rather than purely organic quantum contract wins. The backlog is expanding, but quantum projects are tied to multi-year research milestones that do not always convert to cash on a predictable schedule.
SoundHound is making steady progress, and the voice AI platform is finding traction in ways that are starting to show up in the numbers. Revenue grew at a strong double-digit rate in the most recent quarter, and enterprise deals are accumulating across healthcare and automotive.
For an investor willing to accept significant volatility, IonQ's diversified customer base and expanded manufacturing capabilities make it the slightly more grounded of these two highly speculative bets.

On September 29, the U.S. investment research firm Zacks published an article comparing IonQ and Microsoft (also reprinted on Yahoo Finance). The title was 'Which Quantum Stock Has More Upside in October?' The conclusion was clear: if you are investing in quantum for October, Microsoft is in a better position.
There are two reasons. Microsoft earns significant profits from its core business, and it can use that cash to continue quantum research for a long time. Its stock price relative to sales is also much more stable than IonQ's. While IonQ is growing in both technology and sales, it is operating at a loss and cannot cover the time it takes for quantum to become a viable business with the money it earns itself.
As someone who has the majority of their assets in IonQ, I wanted to skip the article as soon as I saw the title. I could already see the conclusion that my holdings were at a disadvantage. What caught my attention when I opened it was that the distinction between 'a company that can bet on quantum with cash from its core business' and 'a company that cannot generate its own funds until quantum becomes a business' was close to the topic of budget allocation, which I always worry about in my design work. So, I went back and checked the figures from the financial reports mentioned in the article.
When normalized to a full year, Microsoft is much larger
The article lists three months of cash generated by Microsoft's core business (operating cash flow) alongside one year of capital expenditure in the same paragraph. Because the periods are different, it reads as if the amount spent is double the amount earned.
When normalized to a full year, even after subtracting all capital expenditures from the cash coming in from the core business, about $67 billion remains. The cash on hand mentioned in the article also more than triples when short-term investments are added.
According to the article, the majority of capital expenditure is for cloud and AI data centers. Research and development expenses also account for about 10% of sales.
There is no mention anywhere of how much is being spent on quantum. As far as I read in the business description and R&D sections of the annual report (10-K), I could not even find the word 'quantum.' Microsoft's quantum expenses are buried somewhere within R&D or capital expenditures, and the scale cannot be determined from the outside.
For IonQ, at least until the first half of the year, the company's overall figures were almost entirely the figures for its quantum-related business (the SkyWater acquisition was at the end of July).
In the first half of this year (January to June), IonQ reduced its cash from its core business by about $250 million (outflow of operating cash flow). This is a threefold increase from the same period the previous year.
The cash Microsoft earns from its core business is about $500 million per day when divided by the number of days in a year. The cash IonQ burned over half a year is equivalent to about half a day's worth of that. Even when comparing the remainder after subtracting capital expenditures, it does not reach two days' worth.
It is unknown how much Microsoft actually spends on quantum. Even if we assume they were spending the same amount that IonQ burns in a year at its current pace, it would still only amount to about one day's worth of Microsoft's core business earnings. For IonQ, that amount represents the entire reduction in the company's cash.
The proportion of the budget determines the approach
Having worked in circuit design for over a decade, I feel that the way development proceeds is often determined more by the proportion of the total budget than by the amount of money itself.
In terms of circuit boards, the number of prototypes you can run is determined by how much the cost of that prototype accounts for the total budget. If a single prototype is small relative to the whole, you can build, measure, fix, and build again. You can also build two different proposals side-by-side and narrow it down to one after seeing the results. If a large part of the budget disappears in a single prototype, you spend much more time on verification before building, intending to get it right the first time.
A board intended to be completed in one go is also built differently. You include pads left empty without components, places where wiring can be switched later, and extra terminals for measurement. It is a method of building in backup paths on a single board so that if things don't go well, you can escape to another path without having to rebuild. Those who can run multiple prototypes don't have to go that far, as they can fix it in the next version.
Microsoft's quantum approach is closer to the former. Internally, they have chosen a method called topological qubits. It is a method that attempts to imbue the resistance of qubits to failure into the properties of the material itself, a path that almost no other major company has taken. Separately, they also announced in 2025 a plan to build an error-corrected quantum computer (Magne) for Denmark in collaboration with Atom Computing, which uses a different method called neutral atoms. On their own cloud (Azure Quantum), they also allow the use of machines from IonQ, Quantinuum, and Atom Computing. Even if their own method fails, if another company's method succeeds, they can continue to be involved as a partner or gateway (though the terms of their share are not public).
Research into the topological method has been long. Microsoft established its research center for this method in the mid-2000s, which is about 20 years ago now. In 2018, a paper by a group led by one of Microsoft's research heads (who was also a professor at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands) was published in Nature and retracted in 2021. Since then, they released their first chip (Majorana 1) in 2025 and the next chip (Majorana 2) in June of this year, and have set a goal to build a scalable quantum computer by 2029. Opinions among physicists are still divided as to whether a truly topological qubit has been created. In September, the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) became able to independently test the actual machine at Microsoft's facility. The results are yet to be published.
Even after the paper supporting their flagship method was retracted, they released a new chip four years later without changing the method. If the same thing had happened at a company specializing in quantum, I think the conditions for raising money next time would have changed significantly. This is a guess. A company that carries quantum with cash from its core business can wait without changing its method even if it stumbles.
“For as many years as it takes” cannot be verified from the outside
Even so, it cannot be said for certain that a company with a core business will continue to support quantum indefinitely.
As I wrote in a previous article, reports indicate that NEC stopped developing actual quantum computer hardware at the end of March 2026. Alibaba let go of its quantum laboratory in November 2023, and Baidu did the same in January 2024, despite both having core businesses.
In companies with a core business, quantum budgets are decided every year alongside other internal investment targets. In Microsoft's case, what sits next to it is the cloud and AI data centers, which account for the majority of capital expenditure. As long as quantum remains small and inconspicuous, it is less likely to be scrutinized in detail. Once it reaches the stage of scaling up machines toward the 2029 goal, the required amount will increase, and it will become visible within the company.
It is not as if there is no pressure to show results. Microsoft itself has explained that the 2029 goal is half of its original projection. The announcement of Majorana 1 received strong criticism from physicists.
The way things look when they are stopped is also different. Internal decisions are communicated externally only after they are finalized. NEC's withdrawal also came to light through reports rather than a company announcement. Since the quantum budget is not disclosed, it is difficult for Microsoft shareholders to read budget cuts from financial statements. IonQ is the opposite; how much cash has decreased and how many shares have been issued are released every quarter. Because it is visible, bad numbers immediately affect the stock price.
The weaknesses of IonQ pointed out in the article were indeed true when looking at the numbers.
A company that cannot generate its own funds until quantum becomes a business has no choice but to raise the shortfall from the market. In 2025 alone, IonQ raised over $3 billion through stock issuance. Some of this includes warrants that give the right to buy shares in the future at a fixed price. The purchase price is set higher than the current stock price, but if the stock price exceeds that level, these will be exercised, and the number of shares will increase by about 20% from now.
After using cash for the acquisition of SkyWater at the end of July, the cash on hand is said to be about $2 billion. Simply dividing this by the pace of the first half of the year, it is calculated to last about four years. This calculation does not include capital expenditure for SkyWater's factories or costs increased by the acquisition. The rate of cash burn has tripled in a year, and if it continues to increase at this rate, it will be even shorter.
With the acquisition of SkyWater, IonQ also gained revenue outside of quantum. This is contract manufacturing of semiconductors for defense, aerospace, and automotive industries. Of this year's revenue forecast, more than one-third is believed to be from SkyWater. Looking only at revenue, IonQ is no longer just a quantum company. However, SkyWater's gross margin (the percentage remaining after subtracting cost of goods sold from revenue) is around 20%, and it was in the red in the first half of 2026. The current numbers do not show cash from there supporting quantum research.
There is another way to look at it. Even if quantum fails, IonQ might remain as a company with factory and communication/sensor businesses. However, I don't think the current stock price reflects the value of those factories.
In Zacks' own ratings, IonQ was a 'Sell' and Microsoft was a 'Hold.' This rating is explained as an indicator for looking 1 to 3 months ahead, based on which way analysts' earnings estimates have been revised in the past few months.
